issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (including that the SealSaloon.stock attribute should be a final Stock and certain methods are provided by Stock), but the template repository provides an 'Inventory' class that implements the expected behavior while the Stock.java file is empty. The solution also uses Inventory as the type for the shared stock attribute. This naming/type mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) and the presence of an empty Stock.java will confuse students about which class to use or modify and may block them from implementing the design as specified in the problem statement.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the class name consistent across all artifacts. Either (A) rename the provided Inventory class and its usages to Stock (and remove or implement the empty Stock.java accordingly) so it matches the problem statement and UML, or (B) update the problem statement and UML to reference Inventory instead of Stock and remove the empty Stock.java. Ensure SealSaloon.stock uses the same type as the class provided in the template.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Stock class (with methods add, take, findStockIngredient, addToStockIngredients, emptyStock) as the central inventory entity, but the provided template and the reference solution implement this functionality in a class named Inventory. This inconsistent naming (Stock vs Inventory) forces students to map the problem's Stock concept to the Inventory class in code, creating unnecessary confusion when following the specification and UML.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the inventory entity name consistent across all artifacts. Either (A) rename the Inventory class and its files to Stock (and update all references in SealSaloon and other classes), or (B) update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Prefer renaming Inventory -> Stock to match the problem/UML so students can directly map requirements to code.
